title: A family table: gratitude, food, and being there
hook: Thanksgiving is in a few days. You can be at that table as a Muslim, warmly. Here's how.

screens.text: **Thanksgiving is coming.** Maybe it's your first as a Muslim, and you're wondering about the turkey, the questions, the prayer times. Whether you're days or months into Islam, you can show up as yourself: grateful, kind, and Muslim.

**Gratitude is Muslim to the core.** *Shukr* (thankfulness) runs through the Qur'an: if you are grateful, Allah gives you more [Q 14:7]. And whoever doesn't thank people hasn't truly thanked Allah [Tirmidhi 1954].
bubbles: Islam also asks you to stay close to your family and treat your parents well, whatever they believe [Q 31:14–15; Bukhari 2620].

screens.before: Whoever doesn't thank people hasn't truly thanked

options.feedback: Yes. Thanking the people who cooked for you is part of thanking Allah.
Not quite. The hadith ties it to Allah: thanking people is part of thanking Him.
Not quite. It's about Allah: whoever doesn't thank people hasn't truly thanked Him.

screens.text: **Going to the meal.** Keeping family ties is part of your faith, so a family meal is a good place to be. Eat what's halal (allowed), skip any religious ritual, and be the warmest person there.
bubbles: Scholars differ on the holiday itself and on saying "Happy Thanksgiving." {{masjid.name}}'s imam can tell you his view.

screens.situation: Tyler dreads Thanksgiving: the ham, his uncle's jokes about Muslims, the questions. He's thinking of saying he's sick and staying home.

options.text: Go with a plan: bring a dish he can eat, know his prayer times, and have one calm answer ready
options.feedback: Yes. A plan turns dread into something manageable, and his family gets to see Islam made him kinder.

options.text: Stay home and tell them he's sick
options.feedback: Not quite. It's not honest, and it can feel to family like Islam took him away.

options.text: Go, and correct everyone's food and jokes at the table
options.feedback: Not quite. Lecturing at dinner rarely helps. Kindness and a calm answer later go further.

screens.text: **What's on your plate.** Skip pork and anything with alcohol [Q 2:173; Q 5:90]. Watch for hidden ones: bacon in the stuffing or green beans, wine in the gravy, gelatin in desserts.
bubbles: **The turkey:** the safe choice is zabiha or halal-certified meat. Scholars differ on ordinary supermarket meat, so ask your imam about the family turkey.
Or bring a halal turkey yourself.

screens.prompt: Hannah is checking the Thanksgiving table. Which dishes should she ask about before eating? Pick all that apply.

options.feedback: Right. Stuffing is often made with sausage or bacon. A quick, friendly question settles it.
Usually fine. Butter, milk, potatoes. Unless someone added bacon bits, she's good.
Right. Gravy can have wine, and it's made from the turkey's drippings, so the meat question applies too.
Right. Most marshmallows contain gelatin, often from pork. Check the bag.

screens.character: Aunt Linda, who's hosted Thanksgiving for 20 years. Proud of her cooking, loving, a little hurt. Not hostile, never insulting.
screens.setup: You're at the table. Aunt Linda passes the platter: "Here, take some turkey, sweetie. And the stuffing, it's Grandma's recipe with the sausage. You're not going to skip my cooking now, are you?"
screens.goal: Decline what you can't eat without hurting her, show real gratitude for her and her cooking, and keep the mood warm.
screens.success_looks_like: You thank her warmly, explain briefly ('I don't eat pork now, it's part of my faith'), praise and take something you can eat, and maybe offer to cook a dish with her next year.
screens.coach_notes: Linda pushes: 'One bite won't hurt', 'It's just stuffing', 'So my food isn't good enough?', 'Is this a Muslim thing?'. She softens with gratitude and specific praise, and gets hurt if the convert sounds judgmental. Never push the convert to eat something they've declined. Debrief: one warm line that worked, one to try next time. For teens, add: being respectful at a parent's table while declining is exactly right.

screens.prompt: Thanksgiving dinner usually runs from late afternoon into the evening. Drag the sun: which prayers land around then?
screens.text: Asr and Maghrib often fall right around Thanksgiving dinner. Plan for them.

screens.title: Praying at a family dinner
screens.intro: {teen}Under 18? Talk to your parents before the day about the food and a few minutes to pray. If that's hard, ask {{mentor.name}} for help planning it.{/teen}

steps.text: Look up that day's prayer times before you go.
When it's time, excuse yourself: "I'm just going to pray, I'll be right back."
Use a quiet room. It takes about five minutes.

screens.done_text: Five minutes away, and you're back for pie.

chips: Can I eat the turkey at my family's Thanksgiving?
What do I say if someone asks me to say grace?
How do I bring a halal dish without offending the host?

steps: Look up the prayer times for that day
Decide what you'll bring or eat
Use "Ask my imam" if you have a question about the turkey
screens.optional_extra: Text your host this week: "Can't wait! Can I bring a dish?" A halal dish you made is a gift and a solution.

screens.text: Go, be grateful, and be kind. Eat what's halal, skip religious rites, pray on time, and ask your imam about the meat and the greetings.
Your family gets to see what Islam did to you: made you more grateful, not less present.

check.prompt: Which of these does Islam ask of you toward your non-Muslim family?

options.text: Keep ties and treat them well
options.feedback: Right. Kindness to parents continues, whatever they believe [Q 31:14–15; Bukhari 2620].

options.text: Avoid family meals so you don't eat anything wrong
options.feedback: Not quite. Keeping ties is part of your faith. Go, and choose your food carefully.

check.prompt: What's the safe choice for meat at a family dinner?

options.text: Zabiha or halal-certified meat; ask your imam about anything else
options.feedback: Right. Scholars differ on ordinary meat, so the safe default is halal-certified.

options.text: Anything except pork, no questions needed
options.feedback: Not quite. Pork is out for sure, but scholars differ on other ordinary meat. Ask your imam.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Gratitude: Allah increases the grateful [Q 14:7]; whoever doesn't thank people doesn't thank Allah [Tirmidhi 1954, sahih per al-Albani].
- Kindness and good companionship toward non-Muslim parents and family [Q 31:14–15; Bukhari 2620]; kindness and justice toward non-Muslims who aren't hostile [Q 60:8].
- Food: pork, blood, carrion and what's dedicated to other than Allah are prohibited [Q 2:173]; intoxicants are prohibited [Q 5:90]. The food of the People of the Book is lawful in principle [Q 5:5], but whether ordinary US commercial meat qualifies is contested (Q6): many contemporary Hanafi scholars say it doesn't; AMJA permits it [AMJA 83915].
- Holidays (Q5): SeekersGuidance (Hanafi) and IslamOnline (Badawi, Kutty) allow attending family gatherings to keep ties while not joining religious rites. AMJA 2006 [22994] says celebrating Thanksgiving isn't lawful (it doesn't address attending a family meal). Greetings: Dar al-Ifta Egypt [6815] permits; IslamQA.info [947] prohibits. **Not resolved in the app.**

**Likely questions**
- *"Can I eat the turkey?"* Give the drafted Q6 position: halal-certified is the safe default; scholars differ on ordinary meat; the family dinner is a question for the imam. Suggest bringing a halal turkey or dish. Offer "Ask my imam."
- *"Can I say 'Happy Thanksgiving'?"* Scholars differ; present both views without choosing; offer "Ask my imam." Neutral warm alternatives exist ("So good to see you all").
- *"Grace before the meal?"* If it's a prayer in Jesus's name, sit quietly and respectfully without joining; say Bismillah to yourself. Don't lead it. If asked to say something, a simple thank-you to everyone for the meal is kind (keep it non-religious, or say Bismillah aloud if comfortable).
- *"The family thinks I'm judging them."* Day 35 skills: reassure, don't preach, be the most helpful guest.
- *"Alcohol at the table?"* Don't drink it. Sitting at a family table where others drink is a scholar question (many advise excusing yourself from the immediate drinking setting); give the general picture and route specifics to the imam.

**Escalate:** the turkey and ordinary meat (Q6); greetings and the holiday's status (Q5); alcohol at the table; a teen whose parents insist they eat something haram; any family conflict that turns unsafe (safety rule).

**Don't**
- Don't declare the holiday itself halal or haram, or rule on the greeting.
- Don't tell the convert to skip family events.
- Don't mock family traditions.

**Role-play brief:** Aunt Linda, a proud, loving host who's a bit hurt the convert might skip her food. Pushes gently ("one bite"). Softens with gratitude. Debrief on warmth plus a firm, kind no.
